sources.text:
The public site is bilingual, Hebrew and English, so every piece of content needs a translation. Not everything can be translated by a machine: a person's name needs transliteration, not translation, and some fields are sensitive enough that a machine must never translate them.

The product and its business domain are not described here.

The challenge was to run automatic translation without hurting the reliability of the content, so that the model's output never overwrites a person's edit.

Sarah designed and built the pipeline end to end.

A worker with no dependencies runs on a GitHub Actions schedule every 6 hours. It translates only what is missing, using the Claude API, and marks every result as a machine translation.

Translations live in an overlay with a status per field: `machine`, `human` or `rejected`. An editor approves or fixes a machine translation. Once a person has touched a field, the machine never overwrites it.

The field catalog defines, per field, whether machine translation is allowed. Fields marked `human_only` are skipped by the worker.

The workflow uses retry with exponential backoff, concurrency groups so two runs do not overlap, and a manual trigger with parameters.

**Every model output goes through a human approval gate, and never overwrites a person's edit.** This is the principle the whole pipeline is built around.

The pipeline went to production as part of the data-governance platform Sarah built alone, end to end.

This agent is one link where anyone can ask what matters to them about her experience, get an answer grounded in cited sources, and inspect the engineering behind it: the sources, the quality numbers, the decisions and the code.\n\n- **Every claim must come from a source.** The agent may only say what the knowledge base says, and cite it, so retrieval quality is the product, not a detail.\n- **Hebrew and English.** Most visitors ask in Hebrew, while the records are written in English. Plain keyword search fails across languages.\n- **Zero cost, public traffic.** Only free tiers, and no free service whose terms forbid a public app (ADR-0009 rules out the free Gemini tier on the visitor path). Groq quotas cap how many experiments can run in a day.\n- **Numbers, not impressions.** Every design choice is decided by a rule written before the experiment runs, on a labeled dataset, with confidence intervals.\n\nSarah owns the product, the specification and every decision: she wrote and approved the spec chapter by chapter, labeled the evaluation sets, and approved each ADR before it was accepted. She built the system with Claude Code as her coding partner, which is why the commits carry a Claude co-author line.\n\nThe knowledge base is a folder of Markdown records (`portfolio/`) with a strict frontmatter schema, checked in CI by a Pydantic validator, plus a publication check that blocks banned terms in any tracked file. Records are ingested into Neon Postgres, one chunk per record (C4), with `tsvector`, trigram and pgvector indexes. Postgres has no Hebrew dictionary, so text is normalized the same way at ingestion and at query time: final letters become regular letters, and niqqud and cantillation marks are removed. To search, it writes its own English query (Q1) through the `search_portfolio` tool; code strips Sarah's name from that query, because the name pulled generic records to the top. Retrieval is hybrid (R3): a lexical ranking (BM25 and trigrams, fused with RRF) and a vector ranking (multilingual-e5-small, cosine) fused again with RRF, k = 60. Each hit keeps its lexical, vector and fused scores so the trace panel can show why it was chosen. The LLM runs on Groq.\n\nThe UI is Next.js with Hebrew (RTL) and English routes, deployed with the backend in one Vercel project (ADR-0004).\n\nQuality is measured on four datasets: D1 (96 retrieval questions with gold chunks, split dev/test, test never read), D2 (36 adversarial cases), D3 (11 job ads with labeled requirements, including injection attempts) and D4 (12 multi-turn conversations). Database tests run against PGlite in CI.\n\n**Chunking: one chunk per record (C4).** Rejected: a chunk per heading (C1), with or without a context header (C2), and grouped sections (C3). Why: C4 had the highest Recall@5 (0.76 vs 0.46 for C1), significantly better than all three, and the records are small enough to fit (ADR-0010).\n\n**Hybrid retrieval (R3).** Rejected: lexical only (R1) and vectors only (R2). Why: R1 and e5 missed different questions, and fusing them reached 0.88, significantly better than either alone (ADR-0011).\n\n**multilingual-e5-small for embeddings.** Rejected: e5-base and bge-m3 (no better, and slower: bge-m3 ~800 ms per query), MiniLM and Qwen3 (weaker), and Gemini (best on quality, 0.90, but its free tier is not allowed on the visitor path). Why: as good as the larger models in R3, and the smallest and simplest (ADR-0012).\n\n**The agent writes the query, and code strips the name (Q1).** The first Q1 run scored worse than the raw question (0.78 vs 0.88), because the model added \"Sarah Halevy\" to 36 of 50 queries and that pulled the FAQ record to the top. Sarah chose to keep Q1 and strip the name in code, which brought it to 0.87 (ADR-0013).\n\nThe first reranking run reported a median of 16.5 seconds per call, far too slow for a chat. The number was wrong, not the model: Groq's rate limit answered with 429, the client waited and retried, and the timer counted the waiting as part of the call. The fix was to record the wait separately from the call time. Measured that way, the real rerank call takes 1.5 seconds at the median and 1.9 at p95 (31 calls). Latency is now reported without rate-limit waits, and the waits are counted on their own.\n\nOn the D1 dev split, hybrid retrieval with one chunk per record finds the right sources in the top 5 for 0.88 of the labeled sources (Hebrew 0.86, cross-lingual 0.91). LLM reranking (R4) is under evaluation: its first run scored significantly higher, and by the stopping rule written before the run, two more runs decide whether it is adopted. The agent loop, the UI and the hardening are still being built (milestones M4-M6), and this record is updated as each one lands.\n\nMeasured:\n- Recall@5, chunking (C1 → C4, lexical retrieval R1): before 0.46, after 0.76. How it was measured: D1 dev split, 50 questions with hand-labeled gold chunks; paired bootstrap, 10,000 resamples, 95% interval; docs/experiments/retrieval-2026-11-04.md, stage 1\n- Recall@5, retrieval method (lexical R1 → hybrid R3 with e5-small, on C4): before 0.76, after 0.88. How it was measured: Same D1 dev split and bootstrap; stage 2 of the same report; difference significant (ADR-0011)"},{"chunk_id":"git-mcp-server#all","text":"AI agents that debug or explore code need the real, current state of a repository: the working tree, uncommitted changes and the full Git history, not a stale snapshot or a remote API. But an agent that can run Git commands can also change or destroy a repository. grounded-git-mcp is a local MCP server that gives agents that access, while it never runs a write operation on its own.\n\nAgents need real access to the repository to be useful, yet nothing they do may change it without a person's explicit approval, on the exact state that person reviewed. A command that looks like a read can still mutate state, and a Git process can hang on a prompt or run forever.\n\nSarah built the whole server on her own, as a personal project.\n\nThe server is built on FastMCP. It exposes 10 tools (repository info, status, diff summary, log, show commit, grep, blame, conflict detection, propose a command, execute a confirmed command) and 3 read-only resources: the tree at a reference, a file at a reference, and the diff between two references. Tool and resource descriptions are written for the model, as part of the contract that guides it to the right tool.\n\n**SafeGitRunner** is the single point through which every Git command runs. It never uses a shell, always runs in the repository root, and sets a non-interactive environment (no credential prompts, no pager, a fixed locale) so the agent never hangs. Each command has a hard timeout; a stuck process is killed with its whole process tree (on Windows) or process group (on POSIX). Output has a ceiling, truncated deterministically. In read-only mode, only an allowlist of subcommands runs, and flags that can mutate state are blocked, such as `--global`, `--force`, branch or tag deletion, remote changes and config writes.\n\n**Risk classification:** read commands are low risk and run immediately. Write commands are medium or high risk and only go through approval. Network commands are high risk. Destructive commands such as `reset`, `clean`, `rebase` and `push` are critical: the server rejects them, and the agent can only explain what the user should run.\n\n**Approval flow:** proposing a write returns a one-time confirmation token, valid for 30 minutes. The token is bound to the exact command through a SHA-256 hash of its arguments, and to the repository state the user reviewed: HEAD, optionally the branch and a clean working tree, and no conflicts. Execution requires the exact phrase `I CONFIRM <id>`, and fails if the token expired, was used, the hash does not match, or the repository changed since approval. A worker with no dependencies runs on a GitHub Actions schedule every 6 hours. It translates only what is missing, using the Claude API, and marks every result as a machine translation.

Translations live in an overlay with a status per field: `machine`, `human` or `rejected`. An editor approves or fixes a machine translation. Once a person has touched a field, the machine never overwrites it.

The field catalog defines, per field, whether machine translation is allowed. Fields marked `human_only` are skipped by the worker.

The workflow uses retry with exponential backoff, concurrency groups so two runs do not overlap, and a manual trigger with parameters.

**Every model output goes through a human approval gate, and never overwrites a person's edit.** This is the principle the whole pipeline is built around.

The pipeline went to production as part of the data-governance platform Sarah built alone, end to end.

A CV compresses years of work into a few lines that nobody can verify. "Built a RAG system" looks the same from someone who shipped one and someone who followed a tutorial, and most of Sarah's best work was done for employers, so it has no public link. This agent is one link where anyone can ask what matters to them about her experience, get an answer grounded in cited sources, and inspect the engineering behind it: the sources, the quality numbers, the decisions and the code.

- **Every claim must come from a source.** The agent may only say what the knowledge base says, and cite it, so retrieval quality is the product, not a detail.
- **Hebrew and English.** Most visitors ask in Hebrew, while the records are written in English. Plain keyword search fails across languages.
- **Zero cost, public traffic.** Only free tiers, and no free service whose terms forbid a public app (ADR-0009 rules out the free Gemini tier on the visitor path). Groq quotas cap how many experiments can run in a day.
- **Numbers, not impressions.** Every design choice is decided by a rule written before the experiment runs, on a labeled dataset, with confidence intervals.

Sarah owns the product, the specification and every decision: she wrote and approved the spec chapter by chapter, labeled the evaluation sets, and approved each ADR before it was accepted. She built the system with Claude Code as her coding partner, which is why the commits carry a Claude co-author line.

The knowledge base is a folder of Markdown records (`portfolio/`) with a strict frontmatter schema, checked in CI by a Pydantic validator, plus a publication check that blocks banned terms in any tracked file. Records are ingested into Neon Postgres, one chunk per record (C4), with `tsvector`, trigram and pgvector indexes. Postgres has no Hebrew dictionary, so text is normalized the same way at ingestion and at query time: final letters become regular letters, and niqqud and cantillation marks are removed. Embedding models run in process with ONNX Runtime (quantized, CPU).

The FastAPI agent streams answers over SSE. To search, it writes its own English query (Q1) through the `search_portfolio` tool; code strips Sarah's name from that query, because the name pulled generic records to the top. Retrieval is hybrid (R3): a lexical ranking (BM25 and trigrams, fused with RRF) and a vector ranking (multilingual-e5-small, cosine) fused again with RRF, k = 60. Each hit keeps its lexical, vector and fused scores so the trace panel can show why it was chosen. The LLM runs on Groq.

The UI is Next.js with Hebrew (RTL) and English routes, deployed with the backend in one Vercel project (ADR-0004).

Quality is measured on four datasets: D1 (96 retrieval questions with gold chunks, split dev/test, test never read), D2 (36 adversarial cases), D3 (11 job ads with labeled requirements, including injection attempts) and D4 (12 multi-turn conversations). Database tests run against PGlite in CI.

**Chunking: one chunk per record (C4).** Rejected: a chunk per heading (C1), with or without a context header (C2), and grouped sections (C3). Why: C4 had the highest Recall@5 (0.76 vs 0.46 for C1), significantly better than all three, and the records are small enough to fit (ADR-0010).

**Hybrid retrieval (R3).** Rejected: lexical only (R1) and vectors only (R2). Why: R1 and e5 missed different questions, and fusing them reached 0.88, significantly better than either alone (ADR-0011).

**multilingual-e5-small for embeddings.** Rejected: e5-base and bge-m3 (no better, and slower: bge-m3 ~800 ms per query), MiniLM and Qwen3 (weaker), and Gemini (best on quality, 0.90, but its free tier is not allowed on the visitor path). Why: as good as the larger models in R3, and the smallest and simplest (ADR-0012).

**The agent writes the query, and code strips the name (Q1).** The first Q1 run scored worse than the raw question (0.78 vs 0.88), because the model added "Sarah Halevy" to 36 of 50 queries and that pulled the FAQ record to the top. Sarah chose to keep Q1 and strip the name in code, which brought it to 0.87 (ADR-0013).

The first reranking run reported a median of 16.5 seconds per call, far too slow for a chat. The number was wrong, not the model: Groq's rate limit answered with 429, the client waited and retried, and the timer counted the waiting as part of the call. The fix was to record the wait separately from the call time. Measured that way, the real rerank call takes 1.5 seconds at the median and 1.9 at p95 (31 calls). Latency is now reported without rate-limit waits, and the waits are counted on their own.

On the D1 dev split, hybrid retrieval with one chunk per record finds the right sources in the top 5 for 0.88 of the labeled sources (Hebrew 0.86, cross-lingual 0.91). LLM reranking (R4) is under evaluation: its first run scored significantly higher, and by the stopping rule written before the run, two more runs decide whether it is adopted. The agent loop, the UI and the hardening are still being built (milestones M4-M6), and this record is updated as each one lands.

Measured:
- Recall@5, chunking (C1 → C4, lexical retrieval R1): before 0.46, after 0.76. How it was measured: D1 dev split, 50 questions with hand-labeled gold chunks; paired bootstrap, 10,000 resamples, 95% interval; docs/experiments/retrieval-2026-11-04.md, stage 1
- Recall@5, retrieval method (lexical R1 → hybrid R3 with e5-small, on C4): before 0.76, after 0.88. How it was measured: Same D1 dev split and bootstrap; stage 2 of the same report; difference significant (ADR-0011)

AI agents that debug or explore code need the real, current state of a repository: the working tree, uncommitted changes and the full Git history, not a stale snapshot or a remote API. But an agent that can run Git commands can also change or destroy a repository. grounded-git-mcp is a local MCP server that gives agents that access, while it never runs a write operation on its own.

Agents need real access to the repository to be useful, yet nothing they do may change it without a person's explicit approval, on the exact state that person reviewed. A command that looks like a read can still mutate state, and a Git process can hang on a prompt or run forever.

Sarah built the whole server on her own, as a personal project.

The server is built on FastMCP. It exposes 10 tools (repository info, status, diff summary, log, show commit, grep, blame, conflict detection, propose a command, execute a confirmed command) and 3 read-only resources: the tree at a reference, a file at a reference, and the diff between two references. Tool and resource descriptions are written for the model, as part of the contract that guides it to the right tool.

**SafeGitRunner** is the single point through which every Git command runs. It never uses a shell, always runs in the repository root, and sets a non-interactive environment (no credential prompts, no pager, a fixed locale) so the agent never hangs. Each command has a hard timeout; a stuck process is killed with its whole process tree (on Windows) or process group (on POSIX). Output has a ceiling, truncated deterministically. In read-only mode, only an allowlist of subcommands runs, and flags that can mutate state are blocked, such as `--global`, `--force`, branch or tag deletion, remote changes and config writes.

**Risk classification:** read commands are low risk and run immediately. Write commands are medium or high risk and only go through approval. Network commands are high risk. Destructive commands such as `reset`, `clean`, `rebase` and `push` are critical: the server rejects them, and the agent can only explain what the user should run.

**Approval flow:** proposing a write returns a one-time confirmation token, valid for 30 minutes. The token is bound to the exact command through a SHA-256 hash of its arguments, and to the repository state the user reviewed: HEAD, optionally the branch and a clean working tree, and no conflicts. Execution requires the exact phrase `I CONFIRM <id>`, and fails if the token expired, was used, the hash does not match, or the repository changed since approval. Proposals and executions are written to an append-only audit log, and the confirmations file is written atomically.

**Tests:** unit, integration (against a dummy repository) and schema snapshot tests, run in GitHub Actions on every push and pull request. The server was also validated end to end with the MCP Inspector.

**Arguments as a list, never a shell string.** Rejected: joining the command into a shell string. Why: a joined string is ambiguous when arguments contain spaces or quotes, and opens the door to injection.

**Bind the approval to the repository state.** The token is checked against the HEAD, branch and cleanliness the user saw, so a command approved on one state cannot run on another.

**One-time tokens.** Each approval can be used once, so the same approval cannot be replayed.

The server works end to end with Claude Desktop and the MCP Inspector, and an agent can find a regression through history, diff and blame, then propose a minimal fix without executing anything.

turns.answer:
שרה עבדה עם Claude בשני פרויקטים בולטים:

**צנרת תרגום מכונה עם שער אנושי** — היא תכננה ובנתה צנרת שמפעילה תרגום אוטומטי דרך Claude API. עובד ב-GitHub Actions רץ כל 6 שעות, מתרגם רק מה שחסר, ומסמן כל תוצאה כתרגום מכונה. העיקרון המרכזי: כל פלט של המודל עובר אישור אנושי, ולא יכול לעבור על עריכה של אדם. הצנרת עלתה לפרודקשן כחלק מפלטפורמת data-governance שבשרה בנתה לבד, מקצה לקצה. 

**הסוכן הזה (RAG agent)** — שרה בנתה את המערכת עם Claude Code כשותף תכנות, ולכן ה-commits נושאים שורת co-author של Claude. הסוכן עונה על שאלות על הניסיון שלה, עם מקורות וציטוטים, ומבוסס על Postgres, retrieval היברידי (BM25 + trigrams + pgvector, ממוזגים עם RRF) ו-LLM על Groq. 

בנוסף, שרת ה-MCP שלה (grounded-git-mcp) עובד end to end עם Claude Desktop — אבל שם Claude הוא הצד הצרכן, לא חלק מהפיתוח.

output.user: What's the most ambitious thing she has shipped?
output.answer: The most ambitious product Sarah has shipped is a **28‑screen governance center together with a bilingual, offline‑first Progressive Web App**. She designed and built both applications end‑to‑end, along with the governing API they rely on. The system includes a monorepo managed with pnpm and Turborepo, a typed TypeScript API contract of 1,237 lines, a mock‑first development workflow, offline support via a Serwist service worker, vector maps served through PMTiles, and a full suite of 46 automated tests (Vitest and Playwright). Both the internal data‑center UI and the public travel PWA are in production and handle complex features such as conflict detection, real‑time streaming, and multilingual RTL support.

sources.text:
The platform needed two applications on top of the same data. An internal data center, where editors review incoming claims, resolve conflicts and publish. And a public bilingual, offline-first travel PWA in Hebrew and English that works on phones and desktops, and keeps working when the connection drops.

The product and its business domain are not described here.

Two very different applications, built by one person: a 28-screen governance center, and a bilingual PWA with right-to-left Hebrew that works offline.

Sarah built both applications end to end, together with the governance API they work against.

**Monorepo:** pnpm and Turborepo, with two applications and four shared packages (UI, database, auth, utilities). The UI package holds design tokens, a shared Tailwind preset and shared primitives, next to a written spec that lists forbidden patterns and documented exceptions.

**Data center:** 28 screens in Next.js 15 (App Router, React Server Components, Server Actions, streaming). The claims screen is the reference screen, and the others follow its design. It covers the review queue, automatic conflict detection, approve or reject in one click, the full history of every decision, the field catalog, connecting new sources, and reports. Switching tabs is instant, and panels open with streaming.

**API contract:** a typed TypeScript contract of 1,237 lines describes the whole API, with each endpoint marked `LIVE`, `PROPOSED` or `DEPRECATED`. A mock adapter implements the full state machine, so the UI was built and tested before the endpoints existed. Writes carry a version, and a stale version is re-read and retried.

**Public site:** search with filters, area pages, a planning wizard with a scoring engine Sarah wrote, maps, and a form for suggesting new entries, which arrive in the data center as drafts. English is the default, Hebrew is under `/he` with full RTL, the sitemap has `hreflang`, and each language has its own fonts through `next/font`.

**Offline:** a Serwist service worker with precache, CacheFirst with expiry, an offline page, and protection against races during sync. A user can save the map of a whole area to the device (tiles for zoom 11 to 15), and a saved plan survives losing the network. Vector maps use MapLibre with PMTiles: one static archive read through HTTP range requests, with no tile server. Routing and geocoding use OSRM and Nominatim, with no API keys.

**Mobile first:** every screen was built for the phone first. No interaction depends on hover, and tables fold into cards on narrow screens.

**Analytics:** PostHog hosted in the EU, with no cookies, typed events and no personal data.

**Contract first, with a full mock.** The UI never waited for the server: it was built against the typed contract and the mock, and moved to live endpoints as they shipped.

**Static vector maps with PMTiles.** One static archive is served through HTTP range requests.

**Free routing and geocoding.** OSRM and Nominatim need no API keys.

Both applications went to production. Tests: 46 files, with Vitest for logic (the scoring engine, the state machine, translations, retry) and Playwright for full browser flows, including a dedicated suite that cuts the network to check that offline really works, and runs in a 390×844 mobile profile. Before every push, typecheck and all tests must pass. Sarah also ran manual QA rounds on production, screen by screen, while watching the Supabase and Vercel logs, and fixed the bugs they found, such as dead buttons and updates that were not saved because of version conflicts.

Measured:
- Admin screens in the data center: 28. How it was measured: Counted in the repository at the end of the project, 19.7.2026
- Public pages and routes: about 20. How it was measured: Counted in the repository at the end of the project, 19.7.2026
- Typed API contract: 1,237 lines of TypeScript. How it was measured: Counted in the repository at the end of the project, 19.7.2026
- Test files (Vitest and Playwright): 46. How it was measured: Counted in the repository at the end of the project, 19.7.2026
- Commits: 782, from 20.5.2026 to 19.7.2026. How it was measured: Counted in the git history of the repository

sources.text:
A CV compresses years of work into a few lines that nobody can verify. "Built a RAG system" looks the same from someone who shipped one and someone who followed a tutorial, and most of Sarah's best work was done for employers, so it has no public link. This agent is one link where anyone can ask what matters to them about her experience, get an answer grounded in cited sources, and inspect the engineering behind it: the sources, the quality numbers, the decisions and the code.

- **Every claim must come from a source.** The agent may only say what the knowledge base says, and cite it, so retrieval quality is the product, not a detail.
- **Hebrew and English.** Most visitors ask in Hebrew, while the records are written in English. Plain keyword search fails across languages.
- **Zero cost, public traffic.** Only free tiers, and no free service whose terms forbid a public app (ADR-0009 rules out the free Gemini tier on the visitor path). Groq quotas cap how many experiments can run in a day.
- **Numbers, not impressions.** Every design choice is decided by a rule written before the experiment runs, on a labeled dataset, with confidence intervals.

Sarah owns the product, the specification and every decision: she wrote and approved the spec chapter by chapter, labeled the evaluation sets, and approved each ADR before it was accepted. She built the system with Claude Code as her coding partner, which is why the commits carry a Claude co-author line.

The knowledge base is a folder of Markdown records (`portfolio/`) with a strict frontmatter schema, checked in CI by a Pydantic validator, plus a publication check that blocks banned terms in any tracked file. Records are ingested into Neon Postgres, one chunk per record (C4), with `tsvector`, trigram and pgvector indexes. Postgres has no Hebrew dictionary, so text is normalized the same way at ingestion and at query time: final letters become regular letters, and niqqud and cantillation marks are removed. Embedding models run in process with ONNX Runtime (quantized, CPU).

The FastAPI agent streams answers over SSE. To search, it writes its own English query (Q1) through the `search_portfolio` tool; code strips Sarah's name from that query, because the name pulled generic records to the top. Retrieval is hybrid (R3): a lexical ranking (BM25 and trigrams, fused with RRF) and a vector ranking (multilingual-e5-small, cosine) fused again with RRF, k = 60. Each hit keeps its lexical, vector and fused scores so the trace panel can show why it was chosen. The LLM runs on Groq.

The UI is Next.js with Hebrew (RTL) and English routes, deployed with the backend in one Vercel project (ADR-0004).

Quality is measured on four datasets: D1 (96 retrieval questions with gold chunks, split dev/test, test never read), D2 (36 adversarial cases), D3 (11 job ads with labeled requirements, including injection attempts) and D4 (12 multi-turn conversations). Database tests run against PGlite in CI.

**Chunking: one chunk per record (C4).** Rejected: a chunk per heading (C1), with or without a context header (C2), and grouped sections (C3). Why: C4 had the highest Recall@5 (0.76 vs 0.46 for C1), significantly better than all three, and the records are small enough to fit (ADR-0010).

**Hybrid retrieval (R3).** Rejected: lexical only (R1) and vectors only (R2). Why: R1 and e5 missed different questions, and fusing them reached 0.88, significantly better than either alone (ADR-0011).

**multilingual-e5-small for embeddings.** Rejected: e5-base and bge-m3 (no better, and slower: bge-m3 ~800 ms per query), MiniLM and Qwen3 (weaker), and Gemini (best on quality, 0.90, but its free tier is not allowed on the visitor path). Why: as good as the larger models in R3, and the smallest and simplest (ADR-0012).

**The agent writes the query, and code strips the name (Q1).** The first Q1 run scored worse than the raw question (0.78 vs 0.88), because the model added "Sarah Halevy" to 36 of 50 queries and that pulled the FAQ record to the top. Sarah chose to keep Q1 and strip the name in code, which brought it to 0.87 (ADR-0013).

The first reranking run reported a median of 16.5 seconds per call, far too slow for a chat. The number was wrong, not the model: Groq's rate limit answered with 429, the client waited and retried, and the timer counted the waiting as part of the call. The fix was to record the wait separately from the call time. Measured that way, the real rerank call takes 1.5 seconds at the median and 1.9 at p95 (31 calls). Latency is now reported without rate-limit waits, and the waits are counted on their own.

On the D1 dev split, hybrid retrieval with one chunk per record finds the right sources in the top 5 for 0.88 of the labeled sources (Hebrew 0.86, cross-lingual 0.91). LLM reranking (R4) is under evaluation: its first run scored significantly higher, and by the stopping rule written before the run, two more runs decide whether it is adopted. The agent loop, the UI and the hardening are still being built (milestones M4-M6), and this record is updated as each one lands.

Measured:
- Recall@5, chunking (C1 → C4, lexical retrieval R1): before 0.46, after 0.76. How it was measured: D1 dev split, 50 questions with hand-labeled gold chunks; paired bootstrap, 10,000 resamples, 95% interval; docs/experiments/retrieval-2026-11-04.md, stage 1
- Recall@5, retrieval method (lexical R1 → hybrid R3 with e5-small, on C4): before 0.76, after 0.88. How it was measured: Same D1 dev split and bootstrap; stage 2 of the same report; difference significant (ADR-0011)

output.answer: היא ויתרה על מודל הסגמנטציה (UNet) מכיוון שהמערכת רצה על מכונה ללא GPU. המודל היה כבד – האימון שלו דרש זמן בלתי מציאותי וההפעלה המתמשכת הייתה יקרה מבחינת משאבי CPU. בנוסף, המשימה לא דרשה מפת פיקסלים מלאה; היה מספיק לדעת אם יש עשבים ובאיזו חומרה הם מופיעים. לכן היא העדיפה מודל קל ויעיל יותר – MobileNetV3 – שהשיג דיוק מספק והיה מהיר בהרצה על CPU (30‑80 ms לתמונה) .

sources.text:
Images arrive from the field into object storage, and the system needs to tell, for each one, whether there are weeds and how severe they are. The results feed a dashboard that shows the health of the plants (PHI). The system had to run continuously on a machine with no GPU.

There was no local GPU, so a heavy model was not practical, neither to train nor to run continuously. The images come from field conditions, with noise, changing light and small leaves.

The team built a whole smart agriculture system. Sarah built this part, weed detection, entirely on her own, as one component of that system.

Images from the field land in MinIO. The `weed-detector` service fetches each image, runs MobileNetV3 on it, computes bounding boxes, severity and coverage, and writes the results to PostgreSQL. A dashboard reads these results to show the health of the plants (PHI).

**The model:** a pretrained MobileNetV3, with the last layer replaced by a new layer of two classes, weeds and no weeds. This keeps what the model already learned and trains only the final decision.

**Training and evaluation:** the data was split into train, validation and test sets. Loss and accuracy were tracked on every epoch to check for overfitting, and accuracy was measured on the test set at the end. The model was then also checked on new images from MinIO, to see that it generalizes to real data.

The service runs in Docker, on CPU.

**MobileNetV3 classification instead of UNet segmentation.** Sarah started with UNet, a segmentation model that marks weeds pixel by pixel. It performed well, but without a local GPU, training took an unrealistic amount of time, and it is heavy to run. The task did not need a full pixel mask, only whether weeds are present and how severe they are. MobileNetV3 is built for running without a GPU: it is light, fast on CPU, keeps the Docker image lean, and was accurate enough for the task.

The model was accurate enough for an operational task, with high and stable results on the test set, and it held up on new images from MinIO. Each image takes about 30 to 80 milliseconds on CPU, so hundreds of images can run continuously without loading the system. Sarah presented the pipeline in a demo.

Measured:
- Inference time per image: about 30-80ms. How it was measured: Per image, on CPU, on the machine the service ran on. The tool and the date were not recorded.
